paper.title: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions

nodes.text: What are the neural mechanisms of interpersonal guilt and responsibility during social decisions under risk?
nodes.description: The paper investigates how responsibility for a partner's outcomes in risky choices evokes guilt and which brain regions are involved.
nodes.anchor: The neural mechanisms underlying guilt evoked during such situations of social responsibility are still unknown.

nodes.text: How does responsibility for a partner's outcomes influence momentary happiness and its neural correlates?
nodes.description: The study examines whether agency over decisions affecting a partner modulates happiness and identifies neural signals tracking partner reward prediction errors.
nodes.anchor: we aimed to assess whether responsibility for these rewards, that is, taking into account whether the rewards occurred following choices made by the participant or the partner, would also influence variations in happiness.

nodes.text: Do risk preferences differ between Solo and Social conditions?
nodes.description: The paper checks whether choosing for oneself versus for oneself and a partner alters risk aversion.
nodes.anchor: we first verified that participants’ choices were reasonable... then assessed whether these choices and the risk preferences they revealed changed depending on whether participants chose just for themselves (solo) or for themselves and the interaction part

nodes.text: Responsibility for a partner's bad lottery outcomes decreases participant happiness more than the same outcomes following partner choices, consistent with interpersonal guilt.
nodes.description: The guilt effect: happiness drops more when the participant chose the lottery that gave the partner a low outcome, compared to when the partner chose it.
nodes.anchor: When the partner received the low lottery outcome, participant happiness was lower when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery, which we interpret as interpersonal guilt.

nodes.text: The guilt effect is associated with increased BOLD signal in the left anterior insula.
nodes.description: Left anterior insula activation is higher for low partner outcomes after participant choices versus partner choices.
nodes.anchor: Thus, activation in our insula ROIs increased in situations during which participants experienced guilt for low outcomes impacting their partner, compared to similar outcomes resulting from the partner’s choices.

nodes.text: Functional connectivity between the left anterior insula and the right inferior frontal gyrus varies with choice and condition, suggesting the right IFG is sensitive to guilt-related information during social choices.
nodes.description: PPI analysis shows insula–right IFG connectivity strongest when participants make risky choices for themselves and safe choices for both.
nodes.anchor: Connectivity between this region and the right inferior frontal gyrus varied depending on choice and experimental condition, suggesting that this part of prefrontal cortex is sensitive to guilt-related information during social choices.

nodes.text: Computational models incorporating partner reward prediction errors differentiated by decision-maker (participant vs partner) best explain momentary happiness variations.
nodes.description: The Responsibility model (with separate regressors for partner RPEs from participant and partner choices) outperforms Basic, Inequality, and Guilt-envy models.
nodes.anchor: Overall, the Responsibility and Responsibility Redux models explained the data best (highest R2/adjusted R2 or lowest AIC/BIC); a likelihood ratio test revealed that the Responsibility model fitted better than all the other models.

nodes.text: The left superior temporal sulcus tracks partner reward prediction errors specifically when they result from the participant's choices.
nodes.description: Model-based fMRI reveals a left STS cluster responding more to partner RPEs following participant choices than partner choices.
nodes.anchor: A model-based analysis revealed a left superior temporal sulcus cluster that tracked partner reward prediction errors that followed participant choices.

nodes.text: Participants show similar risk preferences when deciding for themselves versus for themselves and a partner, with a tendency toward higher risk aversion in the Social condition only in Study 1.
nodes.description: Risk premiums do not differ; CARA ρ shows slightly higher risk aversion in Social condition in Study 1 but not Study 2.
nodes.anchor: Overall, we believe that we do not have strong evidence of differences in risk preferences across conditions.

nodes.text: In Study 1, happiness after low partner outcomes was lower when the participant chose the lottery (t(39) = –3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.56, BF10 = 32).
nodes.description: Behavioral guilt effect in the behavioral-only study.
nodes.anchor: When the partner received the low lottery outcome, participant happiness was lower when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery (Study 1: t(39) = –3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.56, BF10 = 32).

nodes.text: In Study 2, happiness after low partner outcomes was lower when the participant chose the lottery (t(43) = –2.68, p = 0.01, d = 0.4, BF10 = 3.8).
nodes.description: Behavioral guilt effect replicated in the fMRI study.
nodes.anchor: When the partner received the low lottery outcome, participant happiness was lower when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery (Study 2: t(43) = –2.68, p = 0.01, d = 0.4, BF10 = 3.8).

nodes.text: Left anterior insula shows higher activation for low partner outcomes after participant choices vs partner choices (peak T = 3.95, d = 0.59, 22 voxels, MNI [–28 24 –4], FWE-corrected p = 0.024 within left anterior insula).
nodes.description: Mass-univariate fMRI result confirming insula involvement in guilt effect.
nodes.anchor: We found a weak response in a small cluster within the left anterior insula (peak T = 3.95, d = 0.59, 22 voxels, peak intensity at [–28 24 –4]; Figure 4F). This correction resulted in a p value of 0.024.

nodes.text: In Study 1, the Responsibility model fitted happiness data better than all other models (all LR ≥ 47.36, p < 0.0001).
nodes.description: Computational model comparison in Study 1.
nodes.anchor: The Responsibility model fitted better than all the other models (Study 1: all LR ≥47.36, p < 0.0001).

nodes.text: In Study 2, the Responsibility model fitted happiness data better than all other models (all LR ≥ 77.83, p < 0.0001).
nodes.description: Computational model comparison in Study 2.
nodes.anchor: The Responsibility model fitted better than all the other models (Study 2: all LR ≥77.83, p < 0.0001).

nodes.text: Left STS cluster responds more to partner RPEs from participant choices than partner choices (pFWE = 0.022, T = 4.70, d = 0.53, 100 voxels, MNI [−52 –32 0]).
nodes.description: Model-based fMRI identifies left STS tracking partner prediction errors contingent on agency.
nodes.anchor: We found this effect in one cluster within the left STS (pFWE = 0.022, T = 4.70, d = 0.53, Z = 4.57, 100 voxels, peak at MNI [−52 –32 0]; Figure 4H).

nodes.text: Right IFG connectivity with left insula is highest for risky choices in Solo and safe choices in Social (pFWE = 0.020, T = 4.34, d = 0.80, 115 voxels, MNI [46 16 22]).
nodes.description: PPI analysis shows condition- and choice-dependent insula–IFG connectivity.

nodes.text: Risk premiums did not differ between Social and Solo conditions in Study 1 (t(39) = 1.53, p = 0.134, d = 0.24, BF10 = 0.49); CARA ρ slightly higher in Social (t(39) = 2.27, p = 0.03, d = 0.36).
nodes.description: Risk preference measures in Study 1.
nodes.anchor: Risk premiums did not differ between Social and Solo conditions (Study 1: Figure 2B, t(39) = 1.53, p = 0.134, Cohen’s d = 0.24, BF10 = 0.49).

nodes.text: Risk premiums did not differ between Social and Solo conditions in Study 2 (t(43) = –0.21, p = 0.84, d = –0.03, BF10 = 0.17); CARA ρ no difference (t(43) = 1.40, p = 0.17).
nodes.description: Risk preference measures in Study 2.
nodes.anchor: Risk premiums did not differ between Social and Solo conditions (Study 2: Figure 2E, t(43) = –0.21, p = 0.84, d = –0.03, BF10 = 0.17).

nodes.text: Study 1: Behavioral experiment (N = 40) with risky choice task, happiness ratings, and computational modeling.
nodes.description: Participants performed three sessions outside the scanner; partner was another participant.
nodes.anchor: Forty healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22–31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study)

nodes.text: Study 2: fMRI experiment (N = 44) with identical task inside scanner, plus neuroimaging acquisition and analysis.
nodes.description: Participants performed two sessions in the scanner; partner was an experimenter; fMRI data collected and analyzed with GLM, PPI, and LMMs.
nodes.anchor: 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23–50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study).

nodes.text: Risky choice task with three conditions (Solo, Social, Partner) where risky option is a lottery with independent outcomes for self and partner.
nodes.description: Each trial presents a safe option and a lottery (50/50 high/low). In Social and Partner conditions, lottery played independently for both players. Safe option gives equal outcome to both.
nodes.anchor: participants repeatedly chose between safe and risky monetary outcomes in social contexts. Across conditions, each participant chose for both themselves and a partner (Social condition), or the partner chose for both themselves and the participant (Partner

nodes.text: Icebreaker game to establish positive social bond: blindfolded drawing with verbal instructions and positive feedback.
nodes.description: 15-minute session where participant and partner take turns drawing half a picture while blindfolded, receiving encouragement.
nodes.anchor: participants played an ‘ice-breaker’ game that created a positive social bond between them, increasing the likelihood of feeling empathy and guilt for each other.

nodes.text: Momentary happiness ratings every two trials on a 100-point scale from ‘very unhappy’ to ‘very happy’.
nodes.description: Ratings Z-scored per participant to normalize variability.
nodes.anchor: Every two trials, one ISI after the outcome of the previous trial, participants were asked ‘How happy are you right now?’.

nodes.text: Computational modeling of happiness with exponential decay: Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, and Responsibility Redux models.
nodes.description: Models include certain rewards, expected value, self RPE, partner RPEs split by decision-maker, and inequality terms; fitted per participant.
nodes.anchor: we fitted computational models to each participant’s happiness data. In these models, certain rewards, the expected value of chosen lotteries, reward prediction errors and additional outcome parameters are modelled separately with influences that decay exp

nodes.text: Risk preference estimation via risk premium (logistic regression certainty equivalent) and CARA expected utility model (probit regression with Fechner noise).
nodes.description: Risk premium: EVdiff at 50% risky choices. CARA: exponential utility U(x,ρ)=1−e^(−ρx), ρ estimated via nonlinear least squares.
nodes.anchor: we estimated risk attitudes by calculating a ‘risk premium’... Second, we used an expected utility theory (EUT) approach to calculate a parameter ρ that describes a decision-maker’s risk attitude under the assumption of constant absolute risk aversion.

nodes.text: fMRI acquisition on 3T Siemens TRIO: EPI BOLD, TR=2500ms, TE=30ms, 37 slices, 2×2×3mm voxels, flip angle 90°, FOV 192mm, PAT2.
nodes.description: Structural T1-weighted image also acquired (TR=1660ms, TE=2540ms, 208 slices, 0.8mm isotropic).
nodes.anchor: Imaging data were collected on a 3T Siemens TRIO MRI system... with a repetition time (TR) of 2500 ms, an echo time (TE) of 30 ms, 37 slices with voxel sizes of 2 × 2 × 3 mm.

nodes.text: fMRI preprocessing in SPM12: discard first 5 volumes, realignment, coregistration, normalization to MNI305, resample to 2mm isotropic, smooth 8mm FWHM, high-pass filter 128s.
nodes.description: Standard preprocessing pipeline.
nodes.anchor: Data were then pre-processed and analysed as in previous studies... using standard procedures in SPM12.

nodes.text: fMRI analysis: GLM1 (event-related), GLM2 (computational regressors), gPPI seed-to-voxel connectivity (left insula and left STS seeds), random-effects group models, LMMs on ROI parameter estimates.
nodes.description: GLM1 includes choice, outcome, and condition regressors. GLM2 uses model-derived regressors (CR, EV, sRPE, social_pRPE, partner_pRPE). PPI uses gPPI toolbox.
nodes.anchor: We used the gPPI toolbox for SPM to run seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses.

nodes.text: Ask participants directly about which emotions they felt during the task to link subjective experience with analytical measures.
nodes.description: Future work to validate guilt interpretation by collecting emotion labels.
nodes.anchor: As discussed above, asking participants directly about which emotions they have felt during the different stages of this task would allow us to link subjective experience with our analytical measures.

nodes.text: Test more participants to assess impact of inter-individual personality traits on guilt and responsibility correlates.
nodes.description: Larger sample would enable individual-difference analyses.
nodes.anchor: Testing more participants would allow us to assess the impact of inter-individual variations in personality traits on the experience as well as the behavioural and neural correlates of guilt and responsibility.

nodes.text: Use more trials to allow separate modeling of risk preferences in gain and loss trials per condition and test whether happiness changes affect subsequent choices.
nodes.description: More trials would improve CARA model estimation and enable dynamic happiness-choice analyses.
nodes.anchor: Using more trials in the experiment would allow separate modelling of risk preferences in gain and loss trials in each experimental condition using expected utility models, and could allow testing whether changes in momentary happiness affect subsequent ch

nodes.text: Vary partner identities (friends, strangers, artificial agents) to reveal impact of social discounting on guilt and responsibility.
nodes.description: Manipulating social closeness could modulate guilt effects.
nodes.anchor: Varying partner identities (friends, stranger, and artificial agent) could reveal the impact of social discounting on guilt and responsibility.

nodes.text: Perform functional connectivity analyses for the feedback phase of the paradigm.
nodes.description: Extend PPI to outcome period to study network dynamics during outcome processing.
nodes.anchor: Functional connectivity analyses could also be performed for the data obtained in the feedback part of the paradigm.
